---
title: "Large Gaussian Graphical Models"
---


Gaussian graphical models often contain hundreds of variables, making edge
selection computationally demanding. A graph with 200 variables has 19,900
candidate edges, and repeatedly updating the graph and its precision matrix can
therefore become costly. For such analyses, `bgm()` provides a faster route,
selected by two arguments:

``` r
fit = bgm(y,
  variable_type = "continuous",
  precision_graph_prior = "joint",
  update_method = "gibbs"
)
```

`update_method = "gibbs"` replaces the default No-U-Turn sampler with a
conjugate sampler that redraws an entire column of the precision matrix at a
time. `precision_graph_prior = "joint"` normalizes the prior over the precision
matrix and graph once, globally, rather than separately for each graph. This
puts every term in the edge move in closed form.

Neither option is the default, and the second changes the model being fitted.
Under the joint specification, the graph prior is the edge prior reweighted
toward sparsity. Its inclusion Bayes factors are therefore not interchangeable
with those from the default specification. [Gaussian Graphical
Model](ggm.qmd#sampling-with-the-gibbs-sampler) describes both arguments and
this trade-off.

This page compares the faster specification with two CRAN packages designed
for the same task, Bayesian edge selection in Gaussian graphical models:
**ssgraph** (1.16), which samples the precision matrix under a spike-and-slab
prior, and **modelSelection** (1.0.7), which performs Bayesian model selection
over the entries of the precision matrix one column at a time.

Everything below uses simulated data: Erdős--Rényi graphs with average
degree 3 and p = 50 to 200. Fits were run one
at a time on the same machine (Apple M5 Pro, R 4.6.0, serial reference BLAS),
with each package evaluated at its defaults and at settings recommended in its
own documentation. The full protocol, the rationale for each setting quoted
from the package help pages, and the complete tables are available
[in the repository](https://github.com/Bayesian-Graphical-Modelling-Lab/bgms-docs/tree/main/benchmarks/ggm-comparison).

## Time to a converged ranking

Default run lengths are conventions, and here they differ by orders of
magnitude: bgms runs 4 × 4000 full sweeps, ssgraph runs 5000, and modelSelection
runs 1000 iterations, each visiting about sqrt(p) of the columns. Comparing
default timings therefore compares conventions, not samplers. The relevant
question is how much wall-clock time passes before the edge ranking stops
changing. By that measure, the fast route earns its name.

We measured convergence on ten replicate datasets with p = 100 at each of three
sample sizes: n = 1000, 500, and 200. We ran one chain on one thread per package,
so chain parallelism does not confound the comparison.

Sample size controls the difficulty of the ranking problem. The generator's
per-edge partial correlations are 0.14 by construction, making n = 1000 an easy
case and n = 500 and 200 substantially harder ones, as the converged AUCs below
show. T is the time, including burn-in, required for the inclusion-probability
AUC to come within 0.01 of its converged value. This is the convergence-cost
metric of @VogelsEtAl_2024_bsl. Each grid point is a separate complete run using
the package's own burn-in policy. The table reports the median [min, max] over
the ten replicates:

| n | bgms, raw frequencies | bgms, as shipped (RB) | ssgraph, g.prior 0.5 | modelSelection |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 0.51 s [0.45, 0.76] | 0.50 s [0.45, 0.56] | 13.3 s [3.3, 13.5] | 1.02 s [1.00, 1.05] |
| 500 | 2.8 s [1.5, 5.7] | 0.56 s [0.52, 0.62] | 65.4 s [13.6, 65.9] | 0.94 s [0.89, 0.98] |
| 200 | 7.0 s [3.5, 68.0] | 0.65 s [0.55, 1.04] | 189 s [63, 254] | 0.53 s [0.44, 0.60] |

bgms reaches its converged ranking in seconds at every sample size. Using raw
inclusion frequencies, the like-for-like sampler comparison, the median time is
half a second at n = 1000 and about three and seven seconds at the two harder
sample sizes. Using the Rao-Blackwellized probabilities that `bgm()` reports,
the median is well under one second throughout. The raw frequencies support the
sampler comparison; the Rao-Blackwellized probabilities describe the software
as delivered.

Relative to ssgraph with the matched 0.5 edge prior, the per-replicate ratios
are:

| n | raw vs raw (the sampler claim) | as shipped (RB) |
|---:|---|---|
| 1000 | 18× [6, 30] | 25× [6, 30] |
| 500 | 18× [5, 44] | 114× [26, 126] |
| 200 | 25× [4, 73] | 235× [61, 424] |

ssgraph is slower in all 30 replicate comparisons. The direction is consistent,
but the magnitude at any one sample size is reliable only to within a factor of
two or three. We therefore report medians with ranges rather than single point
estimates.

The difference first appears in the number of sweeps required to reach
convergence. The median numbers of sweeps are:

| n | bgms, raw | bgms, RB | ssgraph |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1000 | 8 | 8 | 100 |
| 500 | 64 | 8 | 500 |
| 200 | 125 | 8 | 1500 |

Each bgms sweep is also cheaper: at p = 100, it takes 8 ms, compared with 39 ms
for ssgraph.

**modelSelection converges within about a second everywhere, and that speed is
real.** It reached the floor of the tested grid at every sample size in all ten
replicates. Its reported time is therefore an upper bound: the short default run
is converged for ranking, not undersampled.

**The converged rankings are effectively tied.** bgms and ssgraph have identical
median AUCs at every sample size: 1.00, 0.98, and 0.87 as the signal weakens.
modelSelection is slightly lower at the two harder sample sizes, with median
AUCs of 0.97 and 0.84, but the ranges overlap. The packages agree on the final
ranking; they differ in how quickly they reach it.

The raw and Rao-Blackwellized results answer different questions. The
Rao-Blackwellized estimator averages a conditional inclusion probability and is
therefore informative before an indicator has flipped. At 8 sweeps and n = 200,
nearly half the pairs have never changed state, yet the Rao-Blackwellized
ranking already matches the long-run result. Exploration is substantially
complete at about 64 sweeps, where the raw estimator converges. Because the raw
estimator cannot converge until indicators move, it automatically reflects the
exploration requirement. Raw versus raw is therefore the defensible sampler
comparison, whereas the Rao-Blackwellized column describes performance as
delivered by `bgm()`.

Several limits apply. The study fixes p = 100 and the average degree at 3.
Because the advantage of the point-mass specification depends on sparsity,
denser graphs may reduce it. The generator also assigns uniform edge strengths
by construction, so the ranking problem lacks the heavy tail of genuinely weak
edges that a G-Wishart draw would produce. Convergence of the AUC does not imply
convergence of inclusion Bayes factors or tail quantities.

Finally, modelSelection is not part of the prior-matched comparison. Its
posterior uses a 1/p edge prior and operates on the correlation scale, so it is
not matched to the posterior used by bgms and ssgraph.

## What a complete run costs

The previous section isolates sampler efficiency. A user also needs to know how
long a complete fit takes under the packages' default and documented alternative
settings. At n = 1000 and p = 200, corresponding to 19,900 candidate edges and
289 true edges, we selected an edge when its inclusion probability exceeded
0.5:

| package | settings | threads | wall clock | selected | true pos. | false pos. | AUC |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| bgms | the call above, Bernoulli(0.5) prior | 4 | 394 s | 382 | 258 | 124 | 0.996 |
| bgms | same call, 2/(p−1) edge prior | 4 | 122 s | 169 | 168 | 1 | 0.996 |
| bgms | same call, one thread | 1 | 1410 s | 382 | 258 | 124 | 0.996 |
| modelSelection | defaults, 1/p edge prior | 1 | 4.2 s | 152 | 152 | 0 | 0.994 |
| modelSelection | empirical-Bayes edge prior | 1 | 24.8 s | 170 | 169 | 1 | 0.994 |
| ssgraph | defaults, g.prior 0.2 | 1 | 3174 s | 260 | 238 | 22 | 0.996 |
| ssgraph | g.prior 0.5 | 1 | 3180 s | 435 | 264 | 171 | 0.996 |
| ssgraph | 2/(p−1) edge prior | 1 | 3276 s | 161 | 159 | 2 | 0.990 |

These wall clocks combine sampler speed with chain-length convention. They
therefore describe complete package runs under the stated settings, not sampler
efficiency in isolation; the previous section provides that comparison. Four
conclusions follow.

**Per full sweep, bgms is faster than ssgraph, and threading does not explain
the difference.** A bgms iteration and an ssgraph iteration represent the same
unit: one full pass over every column of the precision matrix. At p = 200, that
pass takes 96 ms in bgms and 634 ms in ssgraph, a factor of 6.6. The gap grows
with dimension: over this range, the per-sweep cost scales approximately as
p^3.4^ for bgms and p^3.9^ for ssgraph.

The difference follows from the spike specification. ssgraph implements the
continuous spike-and-slab of @Wang_2015_sssl. An absent edge therefore retains a
small non-zero precision entry, and every column update draws a dense
(p − 1)-variate conditional, regardless of how sparse the sampled graph is.
bgms uses a point-mass spike: an absent edge is exactly zero, so a column update
works only through the edges included in the current graph. Even on one thread,
bgms completes 3.2 times as many full sweeps as the default ssgraph run in less
than half the wall-clock time.

**The runtime of bgms adapts to the sparsity it infers; the runtime of ssgraph
does not.** Changing the bgms edge prior from the Bernoulli(0.5) default to
2/(p−1) reduces the p = 200 runtime from 394 to 122 seconds because the resulting
sparser graphs make the updates cheaper. The same change alters the ssgraph
runtime by only three percent. When a sparse graph is expected, expressing that
expectation in the prior produces both a sparser selection and a faster bgms
fit. This effect and the per-sweep difference have the same source: a
point-mass sampler benefits computationally from the sparsity it infers,
whereas a continuous-spike sampler does not.

**The low runtime of modelSelection comes primarily from visiting fewer
columns.** Each iteration visits about sqrt(p) columns rather than all of them,
but evaluates the full conditional of every entry in each visited column. Its
4.2-second default run therefore performs about 3.0 million pair evaluations,
compared with 318 million for the default bgms run, or 107 times fewer at
p = 200.

Its kernel is also efficient. At p = 200, its measured throughput per pair
evaluation is 3.5 times that of bgms. The advantage crosses over near p = 100,
and the bgms kernel is faster at p = 50. modelSelection starts from a glasso
solution and reports Rao-Blackwellized inclusion probabilities, the same
estimator used by bgms. As the previous section showed, its short run is
converged for ranking.

The trade-offs are a different posterior, somewhat lower recall at a matched
threshold, and no exact reproducibility. modelSelection uses a 1/p edge prior
and works on the correlation scale. It recovers 152 true edges, compared with
168 for bgms under a comparable sparse prior. It also exposes no seed, and its
counts vary by about two percent across identical calls. Runs from bgms and
ssgraph are reproducible bit for bit.

**The three packages produce largely the same edge ranking.** Across the full
benchmark, the inclusion-probability AUC exceeds 0.99 in every cell but one:
the modelSelection global regression proposal, with an AUC of 0.975. That
setting also takes 94 times as long as its default and is the only documented
modelSelection setting that reduced performance here.

The packages differ more in where they cut the ranking. Their default edge
prior distributions are 0.5 for bgms, 0.2 for ssgraph, and 1/p for
modelSelection. The prior, rather than the sampler, is what moves the
false-positive count.

These results concern one simulated data family, one machine, and CRAN source
builds. ssgraph documents OpenMP threading, but its CRAN source build on this
toolchain links no OpenMP runtime. It therefore ran single-threaded, as its
CPU-to-wall ratio confirms.


## Rebuilding the tables

Every number on this page is traceable to a seeded runner script. The scripts,
the rationale for each package setting, and the complete tables at all three
sizes are available in
[`benchmarks/ggm-comparison/`](https://github.com/Bayesian-Graphical-Modelling-Lab/bgms-docs/tree/main/benchmarks/ggm-comparison)
in this site's repository. The comparison can therefore be rerun whenever one
of the packages releases a new version. Timings are facts about a machine; the
ratios will travel further than the seconds.
